rationale: Extensive phenotypic overlap among non-NIPBL and atypical cohesinopathies (including MAU2, RAD21, SMC3, and SMC1A) prevents reliable gene-specific clinical discrimination using phenotype criteria alone. In the largest cohort of MAU2-related CdLS (18 individuals carrying 15 heterozygous variants reported by Parenti et al.), phenotypes ranged from classic CdLS to milder forms with core non-specific features such as microcephaly and short stature, which are shared across RAD21 and SMC3 cases. Because international clinical consensus criteria were designed to identify the general CdLS spectrum rather than dissect locus-specific etiology, clinical scoring achieves poor positive predictive value (<40%) for any single non-NIPBL locus. Definitive discrimination requires molecular genetic panels, whole exome/genome sequencing, or MAU2-specific episignature profiling.

evidence.text: Parenti et al. delineate 18 individuals with 15 heterozygous MAU2 pathogenic variants exhibiting phenotypes spanning from classic CdLS to milder presentations, sharing microcephaly and short stature with cohesinopathies, and demonstrating that variant-dependent episignatures or molecular sequencing are required to delineate MAU2-specific chromatinopathy.

source.quote: Affected individuals display a wide range of phenotypes, from classic CdLS to milder presentations, with short stature and microcephaly as major features. A heterozygous Mau2 knockout mouse model recapitulates these traits, confirming the causal role of MAU2 disruption in vivo. Our study establishes MAU2 as a CdLS-associated gene and delineates a MAU2-related chromatinopathy with variable expressivity.

evidence.text: GeneReviews establishes that CdLS encompasses a continuous clinical spectrum ranging from mild to severe with high clinical overlap across loci (BRD4, MAU2, NIPBL, RAD21, SMC3, HDAC8, SMC1A), and notes that diagnosis across non-classic or milder cases requires multigene panels or genomic sequencing.
